PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

This sub-strand builds listening fluency through sport. You will hear the difference between the sounds /ð/ and /θ/, say the sound /aʊ/ and the cluster sk, and use words such as referee, whistle, kit and captain. You will also listen to a short speech, read faces and gestures, and give a short speech of your own.

## Strand 11.0: Sports: My Favourite Game
Sub-strand 11.1.1: Listening and Speaking: Pronunciation and Vocabulary
Suggested lessons: 2

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) listen to short speeches related to the theme for listening fluency
b) apply vocabulary related to the theme in a variety of contexts for self-expression
c) distinguish sounds /ð/ and /θ/ and words from an oral text for listening fluency
d) interpret nonverbal cues correctly for listening fluency
e) realise the importance of listening fluency in oral comprehension

## What this sub-strand covers
• Listening Fluency

## Key inquiry questions
1. How do facial expressions and gestures help us to communicate well?
2. Why should we listen actively to what others are saying?
3. What should we do to make people enjoy listening to us?

## Core competencies
• Creativity and Imagination: This is enhanced when the learner engages in activities such as giving a speech using non- verbal cues.
• Self-efficacy: This is realised when the learner ably interprets the nonverbal cues used by peers in communication.

## Values
• Social Justice is encouraged as the learner accords equal opportunities and shares resources equitably while they watch and give a speech about sports.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Effective Communication skills: These skills are developed as the learner engages in activities such as giving brief speeches.
• Peer Education and Career Guidance: These are enhanced as the learner participates in making speeches in club meetings as well as sporting activities.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner applies the skill of listening in all learning areas.
• The learner also relates the content gained in listening to speeches on sports in learning of similar content in Creative Arts.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 11.0 Sports: My Favourite Game, Sub-strand 11.1.1 Pronunciation and Vocabulary

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Sounds /ð/, /θ/, /aʊ/ and the cluster sk

LESSON 1: SOUNDS /Ð/, /Θ/, /AƱ/ AND THE CLUSTER SK
==================================================

## What you will learn
• Hear and say the difference between /ð/ and /θ/.
• Say words with /aʊ/ and words that begin or end with sk.
• Use sports vocabulary in sentences.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply vocabulary related to the theme in a variety of contexts for self-expression; c) distinguish sounds /ð/ and /θ/ and words from an oral text for listening fluency

## Introduction
Put a hand on your throat and say thin, then this. The first sound is quiet air. The second one buzzes. Mix them up and a listener may hear a different word. Sport talks are full of these sounds.

## Notes
### /θ/ and /ð/
Both sounds are made with the tongue lightly between the teeth, or just behind them. Air passes over the tongue.

For /θ/ the voice is off. It is the quiet sound in think, thank, throw, three, both, mouth, thin and athletics.

For /ð/ the voice is on. You feel a buzz in the throat. It is the sound in the, this, that, they, them, then and there.

Say the two sounds in lists so your ear learns the difference.

- /θ/, voice off: thank, think, throw, three, both, mouth, thin, athletics
- /ð/, voice on: the, this, that, they, them, then, there

A sentence with both sounds: They thank the coach, then throw the ball. They and the and then use /ð/. Thank and throw use /θ/.

### The sound /aʊ/
This sound glides. Start with an open mouth and move to rounded lips, as in how, now, out, about, crowd, shout, round and found. A crowd may shout when a team scores. Keep the glide. Do not squash it into one short vowel.

### The cluster sk
A consonant cluster is two consonants said together with no vowel between them. For sk, say /s/ and slide straight into /k/: skill, skip, skate, score, school, ask, desk. In score and skill the cluster is at the beginning. In ask and desk it is at the end.

### Sports words to use
A match is a game between teams. The captain leads a team. The coach trains the players. The referee controls the match and uses a whistle. Players wear a kit. They exercise and practise so they can win, and they learn how to lose fairly. Athletics includes running and jumping. Netball, football and handball are team games played on a field or court. People cheer from the side. A big sports ground is called a stadium.

Try this oral line and pick out the target sounds: 'They thank the coach, then the crowd shouts as we score with skill.'

## Key words
• referee — the person who controls a match and blows the whistle
• kit — the clothes and shoes a player wears for a game
• athletics — sports such as running, jumping and throwing
• cluster — two or more consonants said together, such as sk in score

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these words: thank, they, throw, the, three, them.

Working:
1. Voice off, tongue between the teeth: /θ/.
2. Voice on: /ð/.

Answer: /θ/: thank, throw, three. /ð/: they, the, them.

### Example 2
Which words have /aʊ/, and which have the cluster sk? shout, score, crowd, ask, now, skill.

Working:
1. /aʊ/ glides in shout, crowd, now.
2. sk has no vowel between s and k.

Answer: /aʊ/: shout, crowd, now. sk: score, ask, skill.

## Activity: Listen, repeat and sort
You will need: Word cards, Audio recording if the teacher has one
1. Listen to the teacher or a recording say words with /ð/, /θ/, /aʊ/ and sk. Repeat each word.
2. Sort the cards into four groups: /ð/, /θ/, /aʊ/ and sk.
3. In pairs, one learner says a word from an oral line. The partner says which sound they heard.
4. Each learner says one sentence that uses a sports word and one target sound, for example: The referee blows the whistle and they cheer.

## Practice
1. Is the sound in think /θ/ or /ð/? How do you know?
2. Write two sports words with the cluster sk.
3. Use captain and team in one sentence.
4. Which word has /aʊ/: throw, crowd or three?

## Summary
• /θ/ is voiceless, as in thank and throw. /ð/ is voiced, as in the and they.
• /aʊ/ glides, as in shout and crowd. sk is a cluster, as in score and ask.
• Sports words such as referee, kit, coach and whistle help you talk about a match.

### Answers to practice
1. /θ/. The voice is off; the throat does not buzz.
2. Examples: score, skill, skip, skate.
3. Example: The captain leads the team onto the field.
4. crowd

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Speeches, gestures and listening fluency

LESSON 2: SPEECHES, GESTURES AND LISTENING FLUENCY
==================================================

## What you will learn
• Listen to a short sports speech and pick out key points.
• Read common nonverbal cues correctly.
• Give a short speech that people can follow with pleasure.

Curriculum outcomes: a) listen to short speeches related to the theme for listening fluency; d) interpret nonverbal cues correctly for listening fluency; e) realise the importance of listening fluency in oral comprehension

## Introduction
A coach can tell a player to stop without a long sentence. An open palm, a shake of the head or a pointed finger does part of the work. Listening fluency means you catch both the words and the signals.

## Notes
### A speech to listen to
Good morning. My name is Amina, and I am the captain of our handball team. My favourite game is handball because everybody touches the ball. We throw, we catch and we pass. The referee blows the whistle, and we listen at once. If we shout over the whistle, we miss the instruction.

Last month we lost a match. I wanted to look at the ground, but the coach smiled and pointed to her ear. That meant 'listen and learn'. We thanked the other team and shook their hands. This term we practise our skills after class. I would like each of you to cheer fairly, pass the ball and keep your kit clean. Thank you.

As you listen, note three facts: the game, what the coach's gesture meant, and what Amina asks the class to do.

### Nonverbal cues
Nonverbal cues are messages without words.

- A smile can mean welcome or 'well done'.
- A frown can mean worry or displeasure.
- A nod means yes. A head shake means no.
- A thumbs-up means approval.
- An open palm towards a player can mean stop.
- A finger pointing to the ear can mean listen.
- Eye contact shows that the speaker is talking to you.

These cues only help if both people share the meaning. If you are not sure, ask. Do not invent a meaning that could confuse a teammate.

### Listening fluency
Listening fluency is following speech at a natural speed and understanding it. You look at the speaker, ignore side talk, and hold the main points in your mind. It matters because a missed whistle, a missed score or a missed rule can change the game and the lesson.

### Making people want to listen
Speak loudly enough, not too fast, and pause at full stops. Look at the listeners. Use one or two gestures that match your words. Stay on the topic. Thank the audience at the end. A three-minute speech is long enough to give a beginning, two or three points and a closing, and short enough to hold the class.

## Key words
• nonverbal cue — a message sent by the face, hands or body, without words
• gesture — a movement of the hands or body that carries a meaning
• listening fluency — the ability to follow spoken language and understand it as it is said
• speech — a talk given to a group, with a beginning, middle and end

## Worked examples

### Example 1
In Amina's speech, what did the coach's gesture mean?

Working:
1. Find the sentence about the coach.
2. She smiled and pointed to her ear.

Answer: Listen and learn.

### Example 2
The referee holds up an open palm towards a player who is about to throw. What is a fair reading of that cue?

Working:
1. An open palm towards someone often means stop or wait.
2. Check it against the whistle if you can.

Answer: Stop or wait. Do not throw yet.

## Activity: Speech with cues
You will need: The speech in the notes, Space to stand in front of a small group
1. Listen as the speech is read or played. Write the game, the meaning of the gesture and Amina's three requests.
2. In groups, recite a short poem or chant about a game you like, using a clear voice.
3. Prepare a speech on your favourite game. Include a beginning, two points and a thank-you. Aim to speak for about three minutes.
4. Use at least two nonverbal cues, such as a smile and a nod, and let the group say what those cues meant.

## Practice
1. Name two facts you learn from Amina's speech.
2. What does a nod usually mean? What does a head shake usually mean?
3. Give one reason listening fluency matters in a match.
4. Name two things that help people enjoy listening to you.

## Summary
• Listen for the main points of a speech, not only single words.
• Faces and gestures add meaning. Check a cue if you are unsure.
• A clear, well-paced speech with a few matching gestures is easier to follow.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: her favourite game is handball; she is captain; they lost a match; the coach signalled 'listen and learn'; she wants fair cheering, passing and a clean kit.
2. A nod means yes. A head shake means no.
3. You need to hear the whistle, the score or the coach's instruction the first time.
4. Any two: a clear voice, the right speed, pauses, eye contact, gestures that match the words, staying on the topic.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 11.1.1 LISTENING AND SPEAKING: PRONUNCIATION AND VOCABULARY
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which word begins with the voiceless sound /θ/?
   A. they
   B. the
   C. throw
   D. them

2. Which word has the voiced sound /ð/?
   A. think
   B. thank
   C. this
   D. three

3. Which word has the sound /aʊ/?
   A. score
   B. crowd
   C. skill
   D. three

4. Which word contains the consonant cluster sk?
   A. shout
   B. mouth
   C. score
   D. they

5. Who blows the whistle and controls the match?
   A. the captain only
   B. the referee
   C. the crowd
   D. the kit

6. In Amina's speech, the coach pointed to her ear to mean
   A. go home
   B. listen and learn
   C. hide the ball
   D. change the kit

7. What does a thumbs-up usually tell you?
   A. Stop at once
   B. Approval or well done
   C. The match is over
   D. Sit on the ball

8. A player shakes their head when you offer the ball. A fair reading is
   A. yes, pass now
   B. no
   C. the whistle is broken
   D. start a new sport

9. Why does listening fluency matter when you hear a speech?

10. Which habit helps an audience enjoy your speech?
   A. Speaking too fast to finish
   B. Looking at the listeners and pausing at full stops
   C. Turning your back
   D. Shouting over every sentence
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 11.1.1 LISTENING AND SPEAKING: PRONUNCIATION AND VOCABULARY
========================================

1. C. throw
   Throw starts with quiet /θ/. They, the and them start with voiced /ð/.

2. C. this
   This buzzes in the throat. The others are /θ/.

3. B. crowd
   Crowd has the gliding sound /aʊ/.

4. C. score
   Score begins with s and k said together.

5. B. the referee
   The referee controls the match and uses the whistle.

6. B. listen and learn
   The speech says the gesture meant listen and learn.

7. B. Approval or well done
   A thumbs-up is a common sign of approval.

8. B. no
   A head shake usually means no.

9. You can follow the words at a natural speed and understand the main points the first time.
   Fluency in listening means understanding, not only hearing noise.

10. B. Looking at the listeners and pausing at full stops
   Eye contact and pauses make a speech easier to follow.
